newsitem.title: BOSNIA: West turns up heat on Balkans but progress slow.
newsitem.headline: West turns up heat on Balkans but progress slow.

text.p: Western powers are turning up the heat in the Balkans as impatience grows with the slowness of the leaders of former Yugoslavia to comply with the peace agreement that ended the Bosnian war.
High level visits by foreign politicians and threats of sanctions have been stepped up, yet nearly two years after the treaty was signed progress is painfully slow, diplomats say.
The Presidents of Serbia, Bosnia and Croatia signed up to a treaty to end the 3 1/2-year Bosnian war, negotiated in Dayton, Ohio, under intense international pressure, in December 1995.
They pledged to turn over indicted war crimes suspects, allow refugees to return home and construct democratic governments. Yet the promises remain hollow.

A NATO-led peace force is due to leave Bosnia in July next year and the United Sates has made clear it wants to see concrete results so its soldiers can return home after already extending their mandate by one year.

At a NATO summit in Portugal in May, Western allies ordered the still-hostile Bosnian factions to comply with the accords or face sanctions in their toughest ultimatum since the peace treaty was signed.
"There has been a period of build up of impatience," one Western diplomat said on Friday.
"(The allies) are looking at the deadline of next summer. Some people are saying they are determined to withdraw and others are saying hold on.

"It was clear to a lot of people that they may have a difficult choice either to delay (the withdrawal), to put heavy pressure on to accelerate things or to leave Bosnia-Hercegovina without enough confidence that it is stable enough to manage on its own," he told Reuters.
Next week the architect of the Dayton agreement, former U.S. assistant secretary of state Richard Holbrooke, will return to his old stamping ground with an American delegation to press for action.
His visit closely follows that of British Foreign Minister Robin Cook and a regional tour by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
Both fresh in office, Cook and Albright have pledged to make the Balkans a focus of their foreign policy.

The aim of sending the U.S. team to Bosnia "is to send a very strong signal to the parties of our very strong expectation that they get with it on Dayton implementation," State Department spokesman James Foley said this week.
Diplomats say donor countries providing aid for Bosnia's reconstruction are also growing frustrated at the slow pace of change.
"The faster they get on with it the more money they are going to get," said one.

NATO commander General Wesley Clark said the alliance-led force (SFOR) would stick to a tougher policy towards indicted war criminals despite Bosnian Serb attacks on international observers and soldiers.
The revenge attacks came after British forces arrested a Bosnian Serb war crimes suspect and killed another who resisted arrest last month.
"Let there be no misunderstanding. SFOR will fulfil its mandate in every respect. There is no turning back," said Clark, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander.
"There is more pressure being applied but it actually isn't working right now," said United Nations International Police Task Force spokesman Alex Ivanko.
He described Holbrooke as a "pushing force" who would try to revive civilian aspects of the Dayton agreement.
The West's reliance on the region's presidents to hand over indicted criminals has not worked and refugees are still not able to return home over ethnic boundary lines.
The Bosnian government failed to meet deadlines set at the NATO summit on introducing new laws on citizenship and will face penalties if it does not comply soon.
Out of 78 war crimes suspects indicted by the international tribunal, 66 are still at large.
"This issue will not go away," Cook said during his visit.
But as a Western diplomat in Sarajevo said, "it is proving difficult to move forward".
